explanation: Some - Rooted in the ancient proverb "cloth takes the color it is dipped in", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value good company, careful upbringing and the influences one lets soak in.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and the 1809 Kamikiyoto village register, written in kana そめ. Conventional kanji 染 (some, to dye), a plain kun reading; also read as the beginning of something, as in someru. Commoner register name, not a court name. Pronounced so-me, two syllables, not like the English word.

name: Sawa
explanation: Sawa - With origins in the legend of the Marsh Maiden, who guided a lost Imperial survey party through a fen by walking ahead on ground only she could see, this name evokes a sense of local wisdom, patience and hidden paths. It appeals to those who admire knowledge that comes from a place rather than a book.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka), written in kana さわ. Conventional kanji 沢 (sawa, marsh, mountain stream). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Onobu
explanation: Onobu - This name is inspired by the natural element of the spring shoot, symbolizing growth that reaches upward toward the light. It is often chosen for its connection to new bamboo and young rice and its representation of steady, unforced development.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Nobu, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 伸 (nobu, to extend, to grow), the reading matching the explanation; 信 (nobu, trust, faith) is the other common spelling and the registers wrote the base in kana. Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Okichi
explanation: Okichi - A name derived from the fusion of "good" and "omen", reflecting a balance between what one hopes for and what one is given. It is often embraced by those who strive for luck earned through cheerful diligence.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Kichi, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 吉 (kichi, good fortune, auspicious), an on reading used directly as a name; the two senses in the explanation are both carried by that single character. Commoner register name, not a court name. Modern association: Tojin Okichi, the historical geisha of Shimoda linked in legend to the American consul Townsend Harris.

name: Ema
explanation: Ema - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of votive tablet painting, this name represents the small wooden plaques painted with horses and hung at shrines to carry a prayer to the Fortunes. It is often chosen by those who appreciate a wish made visible and have a deep respect for the shrine painters whose horses are meant to be ridden by the kami.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a religious object name of the kind Edo commoners bore (compare Kesa). Kanji 絵馬: 絵 (e, picture) + 馬 (ma, horse, on reading), read Ema, the ordinary word for a shrine votive tablet. Commoner style, not a court name. Modern association: Ema is now a popular Japanese given name, usually with other kanji and influenced by the Western Emma.

name: Kuniko
explanation: The name Kuniko is associated with the famous Oath of the Provinces, in which the daimyo of every province swore before the Emperor to hold their lands as stewards rather than owners. Those who choose this name try to embody values of duty to the realm, stewardship and loyalty above self-interest.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: Nanbokucho and Muromachi court lists, written 國子 (the older form of 国). Kanji 國 (kuni, country, province) + 子 (ko, child), kun reading Kuniko; the on reading would be Kokushi. Court -ko name, but -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting; Kuniko was also a common twentieth-century given name.

name: Sono
explanation: The name Sono is inspired by the Garden of the Nine Pines, known for its walled orchards and paths raked fresh every dawn. The name reflects the ordered abundance of the place and is often chosen by those who value cultivation, patience and beauty that is tended rather than found.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana その. Conventional kanji 園 (sono, garden, orchard). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Kunishi
explanation: Kunishi - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Realm's Founding, an event that emphasizes the unity of the provinces under the Emperor and the shared duties of every household to the whole. People choose this name to reflect their values for civic loyalty, order and belonging to something larger than a village.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name given here in its on reading: 邦子内親王, a Kamakura imperial princess on Japanese Wikipedia's list of empresses. Kanji 邦 (ho, kuni, country, realm) + 子 (shi, child); the kun reading is Kuniko, and the on reading Kunishi is a mixed reading (kun for 邦, on for 子) of the kind conventionally used for court women's -ko names. Court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Ebi
explanation: Ebi - This name represents the shrimp, bent-backed and long-whiskered like an old woman, and is often chosen by those who are born to fishing families or who are expected to live to a great and cheerful old age.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a creature name of the kind Edo commoners bore (compare Tora, Kame, Tsuru). Kanji 海老 (umi, sea + oi, old; read together as ebi, a jukujikun reading), the shrimp or lobster, a New Year longevity symbol because of its bent back and long whiskers. The reading is stylized in that it does not follow the individual characters. Commoner style, not a court name; as a personal name it is playful and would suit a fisher family or a nickname.

name: Uneme
explanation: Uneme - This name means "palace maiden". It represents the young women sent from the provinces to serve at the Imperial table, and the honor a family gains by having a daughter chosen.
notes: Not attested as a personal name in our sources; constructed from a real pre-modern court title. Kanji 采女 (uneme, a jukujikun reading), the ancient office of a provincial girl sent to serve in the Imperial palace; the reading does not follow the characters individually. Title-derived rather than a register or court personal name; in Rokugan it would suit a girl named for a relative who served at court, or a nickname that stuck.

name: Kusu
explanation: Kusu means "camphor tree" or "long life", which can suggest the great fragrant evergreen that outlives whole villages or the plain wish that a child endure. People with this name may be sturdy, sweet-natured and slow to change.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists and Edo village registers (1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana くす. Conventional kanji 楠 (kusu, camphor tree) or the phonetic 久寿 (ku, long-lasting + su, longevity). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Shimo
explanation: Shimo can be written with two different kanji. One means "frost", and the other means "below". The choice of kanji could reflect the circumstances of the birth, such as a girl born on the first frosty morning of autumn or the youngest daughter of a lower household.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1671 Tochii, 1774 Noshio), written in kana しも. Conventional kanji 霜 (shimo, frost) or 下 (shimo, below, lower). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Tsune
explanation: Tsune - A name that means "constant", evoking a woman who is the same in famine and in feast, whose word given once holds for life.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the commonest: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana つね. Conventional kanji 常 (tsune, constant, usual, everyday). Commoner register name, not a court name; also a common element in samurai men's nanori (Tsunemoto, Tsunenaga).

name: Zeni
explanation: Zeni chose their name in honor of the famous Yasuki Zeni, who kept a rice merchant's books so exactly that a magistrate's audit found not one copper unaccounted for and cleared the whole street of suspicion.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of an object name of the kind Edo townspeople bore (compare Kane, Tama). Kanji 銭 (zeni, a copper coin, small money), an ordinary kun reading. Commoner style, a merchant-quarter name rather than a court name; blunt to the point of comedy, which suits a Yasuki or a market family.

name: Chikako
explanation: Chikako was a deity that was said to have taken the form of a mother to nurse an abandoned infant Emperor after the palace had been burned.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: Nanbokucho and Muromachi court lists, written 親子. Kanji 親 (chika, intimate, close; also oya, parent) + 子 (ko, child), kun reading Chikako; the on reading would be Shinshi. Court -ko name, but -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting; Chikako is also a familiar modern given name.

name: Tomi
explanation: Tomi - Derived from the phrase "wealth is a full granary and a full house", this name embodies the idea of prosperity measured in rice and children rather than coin. It is often associated with those who manage a household well and make a little go a long way.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima), where the register wrote the fuller form とみへ (Tomie) in kana. Conventional kanji 富 (tomi, wealth, abundance). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: San
explanation: San - Composed of the elements "three" and "line", the three level strokes of the character, this name symbolizes heaven, earth and humanity standing in order. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of completeness, balance and a third daughter welcomed as warmly as the first.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and among the very commonest: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100, and Edo village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana さん. Conventional kanji 三 (san, three), often given to a third daughter; the two elements in the explanation are a gloss on the strokes of that single character. Commoner register name, not a court name. Note that san is also the everyday honorific suffix, so Osan was the usual form of address.

name: Oshige
explanation: Oshige - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Widow's Mulberry, in which a farm wife whose fields had been burned in a clan war nursed a single scorched mulberry stump until it grew thick enough to feed a whole village's silkworms. It reflects qualities such as stubborn growth, patience, and quiet abundance.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Shige, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Shige is how such a woman was actually addressed. Conventional kanji 茂 (shige, "luxuriant, thriving"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Juzu
explanation: Juzu - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A hundred beads, one string", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value devotion, the unity of a family or temple, and the humility of counting one's prayers.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of an object name of the kind Edo commoners bore (compare register names Nabe "pot" and Kura "storehouse"). Kanji 数珠 (juzu), the Buddhist prayer beads, read with its ordinary on-readings. A commoner-style name with a devotional, temple-household flavor rather than a court name.

name: Okuma
explanation: Okuma - With origins in the legend of the Bear Mother of the northern hills, who carried a lost samurai child on her back through a winter storm to the gate of his family's keep, this name evokes a sense of fierce protectiveness and rough-hewn strength. It appeals to those who admire loyalty that asks nothing in return.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kuma, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kuma is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 熊 (kuma, "bear"), a plain kun reading; animal names of this kind were common among Edo villagers. A commoner register name. Unrelated to the modern surname Okuma (大隈), which uses different characters.

name: Kuno
explanation: Kuno - Stemming from the word "hisashii", which denotes something long-lasting and enduring, this name embodies the spirit of constancy through the years. It resonates with those who are steady, patient, and slow to change their loyalties.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo village registers (1804 Nishitomioka, 1825 Kano), where it was written in kana as くの. The most conventional kanji spelling is 久乃 (ku "long-lasting, enduring" + the phonetic 乃 no), the standard form for register names ending in -no. A commoner register name.

name: Satoko
explanation: Satoko - This name is inspired by the natural element of the home village with its fields and hedgerows, symbolizing the ground a person is rooted in. It is often chosen for its connection to the ancestral land and its representation of belonging, loyalty to one's kin, and the comfort of familiar places.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 里子, read in its kun form Satoko; the on-reading is Rishi. 里 means "village, hometown" and 子 is the standard feminine "child" suffix. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste. In modern Japanese the same characters also spell the common noun satogo, "foster child", which readers may notice.

name: Botan
explanation: Botan - A name derived from the fusion of "stalwart" and "cinnabar red", reflecting a balance between sturdiness and splendor. It is often embraced by those who strive for a beauty that does not wilt at the first cold wind.
notes: Attested name: appears in a list of geisha professional names, period not recorded, written in kana as ぼたん. Conventional kanji 牡丹 (botan, "peony"), whose characters are 牡 "male, robust" and 丹 "cinnabar red"; the flower name is read with its ordinary on-readings. A plant name of the kind commoners and entertainers bore, not a court name.

name: Kaede
explanation: Kaede - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of ink painting, this name represents the maple leaf that painters render in a single sweep of the brush. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the economy of a perfect stroke and have a deep respect for masters who capture a whole autumn in one leaf.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: recorded in a Sengoku-period article on samurai women's names (sengokudaimyo). Conventional kanji 楓 (kaede, "maple"), a plain kun reading. A samurai-household woman's name of the plant-name type rather than a court -ko name. Kaede is a popular modern given name and appears widely in anime and games.

name: Nabe
explanation: The name Nabe is associated with the famous Winter of the Shared Pot, in which a river village cut off by snow survived by cooking every household's last rice in one great cauldron at the shrine and dividing it evenly among the villagers. Those who choose this name try to embody values of generosity, fair dealing, and the warmth of a full hearth.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo name lists and in the 1671 Tochii village register. Kanji 鍋 (nabe, "cooking pot"), a plain kun reading; household-object names of this kind were normal for commoner women. A commoner register name.

name: Nobuko
explanation: The name Nobuko is inspired by the Bridge of Oaths on the Imperial road, known for its stone rails carved with the names of magistrates who swore to keep the crossing honest. The name reflects the trustworthiness of the place and is often chosen by those who value sincerity, kept promises, and a reputation that can bear weight.
notes: Attested court name: borne by Heian empresses and imperial consorts on Japanese Wikipedia and listed among Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) court women. Kanji 信子, read in its kun form Nobuko; the on-reading is Shinshi. 信 means "faith, trust, sincerity" and 子 is the feminine suffix. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste. Nobuko was a very common given name in twentieth-century Japan.

name: Koboshi
explanation: Koboshi - This name represents a little acolyte, the small child who sweeps the temple steps, and is often chosen by those who are raised near a shrine or monastery or who are expected to serve the Fortunes with humble, cheerful labor.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of commoner women, recorded as 小法師女, that is "the woman Koboshi", with 女 marking her sex rather than forming part of the name. Kanji 小法師 (koboshi, "little priest, young acolyte"), read with its ordinary readings; it began as an affectionate nickname of the kind medieval commoners bore. A commoner name, not a court name.

name: Sue
explanation: Sue - This name means "the last one". It represents a family's hope that a youngest daughter closes the line of births in good health, and the settled contentment of a household that feels complete.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the most common of all: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana as すへ or すゑ. Conventional kanji 末 (sue, "end, last"), a plain kun reading; it was commonly given to a youngest daughter. A commoner register name. Its resemblance to the English name Sue is coincidental.

name: Saru
explanation: Saru means "monkey" or "to go away", which can suggest nimble cleverness or the driving-off of misfortune. People with this name may be quick-witted, restless, and hard to keep hold of.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in the 1564 Sugaura register and in early-Edo name lists, written both in kana (さる) and as 猿. Kanji 猿 (saru, "monkey"), a plain kun reading; the name was also chosen for its pun on saru "to depart", so that illness would leave the child. A commoner register name.

name: Tsunako
explanation: Tsunako can be written with two different kanji. One means "to hold together, a binding cord", and the other means "a main rope, a guiding principle". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family hoped she would hold fast to, such as the unity of a household or the rules of proper conduct.
notes: Attested court name: borne by a late-Edo imperial consort, Konoe Tsunako (近衛維子), on Japanese Wikipedia's lists of empresses and consorts. Given name 維子, read in its kun form Tsunako (the same name is also read Koreko); the on-reading is Ishi. 維 means "to bind, to hold together" and 子 is the feminine suffix; the alternative spelling 綱子 uses 綱 "rope, principal cord". A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Juna
explanation: Juna - This name signifies a wish for long life carried lightly, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values endurance, good health, and a gracefulness that outlasts hardship.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-mora name built on an auspicious element, like the Edo register names Kiku and Tora. Kanji 寿奈 (ju "long life, felicity" + the phonetic 奈 na), both ordinary readings; be aware the -na ending sounds more modern than most register names. A commoner-style name.

name: Tama
explanation: Tama - A name that means "jewel", evoking something small, precious, and polished by care until it shines.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo name lists, passenger lists, and village registers (1774 Noshio, 1825 Kano). Kanji 玉 (tama, "jewel, gem, ball"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name. Tama is also the stock name for a pet cat in Japan.

name: Tora
explanation: Tora chose their name in honor of the famous Matsu Tora, who held a mountain ford alone for a night and a day against raiders so that her village's rice could be carried to safety behind her.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the most common: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto), written in kana (とら) and as 虎. Kanji 虎 (tora, "tiger"), a plain kun reading; the tiger was an auspicious guardian animal for girls. A commoner register name.

name: Yae
explanation: Yae was a deity that was said to have folded the mountain cherry's petals eight times over after a mortal gardener wept that one thin layer of blossom was too little beauty for so short a spring.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo village registers (1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya) record it in kana as やゑの (Yaeno), of which Yae is the base form. Conventional kanji 八重 (yae, "eightfold, many-layered", as in double-flowered blossoms), a standard kun reading. A commoner register name. Niijima Yae, the Bakumatsu-era defender of Aizu, is a famous historical bearer.

name: Muneko
explanation: Muneko - Derived from the phrase "carry on the line", this name embodies the idea of a daughter as the keeper of her ancestors' way. It is often associated with those who tend the family shrine, remember the old names, and hold the household to its founding vows.
notes: Attested court name: borne by a Heian empress on Japanese Wikipedia's list of empresses and listed among Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) court women. Kanji 宗子, read in its kun form Muneko; the on-reading is Soshi. 宗 means "lineage, ancestral line, sect" and 子 is the feminine suffix. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Motoko
explanation: Motoko - Composed of the elements "endowment" and "child", this name symbolizes a daughter born with every gift her house could provide. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of natural talent, good resources, and a foundation on which greatness can be built.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 資子, read Motoko; the on-reading is Shishi. 資 means "resources, endowment, capital" and 子 is the feminine suffix; moto is a nanori (name-only) reading of 資, so this is a stylized reading of the kind court names often carry. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste. Modern bearers usually write Motoko as 素子 or 元子, as with Kusanagi Motoko of Ghost in the Shell.

name: Mume
explanation: Mume - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Plum That Bloomed in the Snow, in which a courtier exiled to a frozen province found a single plum tree flowering beside the road and took it as a sign to keep his honor through his disgrace. It reflects qualities such as fortitude, early courage, and beauty that arrives before the thaw.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the most common: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1804 Nishitomioka, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya). Kanji 梅 ("plum"); mume is the older pronunciation of ume, preserved in the registers, so the reading is archaic rather than stylized. A commoner register name.

name: Tsuruo
explanation: Tsuruo - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The crane lives a thousand years", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value longevity, dignified bearing, and fidelity to a single mate for life.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 鶴王 (tsuru "crane" + o "king, sovereign"), both ordinary readings; the -o (王) suffix was a genuine medieval naming element for court women alongside -ko, and it reads oddly to modern ears, so flag it as archaic. A court name; in this setting the style suits any caste.

name: Oyoshi
explanation: Oyoshi - With origins in the legend of Yoshi of the Lucky Ferry, who is said to have rowed a Fortune disguised as a beggar across a flooded river for no fee and was repaid with a lifetime of good catches, this name evokes a sense of good fortune earned through kindness. It appeals to those who admire generosity that expects nothing back.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Yoshi, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Yoshi is how such a woman was actually addressed. Conventional kanji 吉 (yoshi, "good luck, auspicious"), a standard kun reading, though 良 "good" was also used. A commoner register name.

name: Chise
explanation: Chise - This name is inspired by the natural element of a river's countless shallows, symbolizing the many small crossings a life is made of. It is often chosen for its connection to running water and its representation of adaptability, persistence, and the way a stream finds its path around every stone.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in passenger lists and the 1837 Matsushima village register, written in kana as ちせ. Conventional kanji 千瀬 (chi "thousand" + se "shallows, rapids"), both ordinary kun readings. A commoner register name. Hatori Chise of The Ancient Magus' Bride is a modern pop-culture bearer.

name: Okame
explanation: Okame - A name derived from the fusion of "the tortoise's long life" and "its patient steadiness", reflecting a balance between endurance and calm. It is often embraced by those who strive for a life that outlasts every storm by refusing to hurry through it.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kame, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kame is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 亀 (kame, "tortoise"), a plain kun reading; the tortoise is the emblem of longevity. A commoner register name. Okame is also the name of the round-cheeked comic mask of Japanese folk theater (also called Otafuku), a real association any Japanese reader would make.

name: Kura
explanation: The name Kura is associated with the famous Levy of the Sealed Storehouses, in which a provincial governor refused to open the granaries to a corrupt tax collector's men until the Emperor's own seal arrived, and was vindicated when the collector's warrant proved forged. Those who choose this name try to embody values of prudence, stewardship, and firmness in guarding what has been entrusted to them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, and village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana as くら. Conventional kanji 倉 (kura, "storehouse, granary"), a plain kun reading; a wish that the house never lack stores. A commoner register name.

name: Enyo
explanation: The name Enyo is inspired by the Temple of Ten Thousand Threads in the eastern hills, known for its cords of red silk that pilgrims tie between the pillars to mark the bonds they owe to others. The name reflects the connectedness of the place and is often chosen by those who value loyalty, obligation honestly kept, and the ties that hold a village together.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a Buddhist-flavored two-character name mixing an on-reading with a kun-reading, of the kind temple-raised girls sometimes bore. Kanji 縁世 (en "karmic bond, connection" + yo "world, generation"), both ordinary readings, though the combination is unusual and should be treated as stylized. A commoner-style name.

name: Ayu
explanation: Ayu - This name pays tribute to the Summer River Festival, an event that emphasizes the sweetfish run, when whole villages wade the shallows with nets and the first catch is offered at the riverside shrine. People choose this name to reflect their values for seasonal abundance, communal labor, and gratitude to the river spirits.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of an animal name of the kind Edo commoners bore (compare register names Tora "tiger", Kame "tortoise", Saru "monkey"). Kanji 鮎 (ayu, "sweetfish"), a plain kun reading. A commoner-style name. Ayu is a fairly common modern given name and the nickname of singer Hamasaki Ayumi.

name: Ochiyo
explanation: Ochiyo - This name represents a thousand generations and is often chosen by those who are the daughters of long-established farming houses or who are expected to carry the family line forward for ages to come.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Chiyo, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Chiyo is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 千代 (chi "thousand" + yo "generations, ages"), both ordinary kun readings. A commoner register name.

name: Sukeko
explanation: Sukeko - This name means "helping child". It represents a daughter raised to be her family's support, the one who steadies the household when others falter.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 相子, read Sukeko; the on-reading is Soshi. 相 means "to aid, a minister; mutual" and 子 is the feminine suffix; suke is a nanori (name-only) reading of 相, so flag it as a stylized court reading. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Itoko
explanation: Itoko means "thread" or "beloved", which can suggest the fine silk a household spins or the tender word a parent uses for a cherished child. People with this name may be delicate, dear to those around them, and quietly essential to the pattern of a family.
notes: Attested name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women and in Azuchi-Momoyama name lists, recorded as いと子. Conventional kanji 糸子 (ito "thread" + the feminine suffix 子), a plain kun reading; the pun on itoshi "beloved" is traditional. A court -ko name that later appears among samurai households; in this setting -ko suits any caste. The name is a homophone of itoko, "cousin", which Japanese readers notice.

name: Oyuki
explanation: Oyuki can be written with two different kanji. One means "snow", and the other means "happiness". The choice of kanji could reflect the season and hopes of her birth, such as a daughter born in the first snowfall or one wished a life of good fortune.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Yuki, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Yuki is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 雪 (yuki, "snow") is the conventional spelling, with 幸 (yuki, "happiness, good fortune") the traditional alternative; both are standard kun readings. A commoner register name. Oyuki is also the snow-woman of the Yuki-onna ghost tale as told by Lafcadio Hearn.

name: Naka
explanation: Naka - This name signifies good relations between kin and neighbors, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values harmony, mediation, and the peace of a village that settles its quarrels over tea.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and among the most common: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and the 1837 Matsushima register, written in kana as なか. The most conventional kanji is 仲 (naka, "relations, harmony between parties"), with 中 (naka, "middle", for a middle daughter) an equally traditional spelling. A commoner register name.

name: Miya
explanation: Miya - A name that means "shrine", evoking the hush of a sacred precinct and a child placed under the Fortunes' protection.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists and village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka), written in kana (みや) and as 宮. Kanji 宮 (miya, "shrine, palace"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name.

name: Anzu
explanation: Anzu chose their name in honor of the famous Doji Anzu, who planted an orchard of apricot trees along a famine road so that no traveler on it would go hungry in spring again.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a plant name of the kind Edo commoners bore (compare register names Mume "plum", Kiku "chrysanthemum", Matsu "pine"). Kanji 杏 (anzu, "apricot"), its ordinary reading. A commoner-style name. Anzu is a popular modern given name.

name: Chima
explanation: Chima was a deity that was said to have scattered a thousand true words across the Empire after a lying magistrate's speech caused a river to run backward.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo name lists, written in kana as ちま. The registers give no kanji; the most conventional reconstruction is 千真 (chi "thousand" + ma "truth"), both ordinary readings, but treat the spelling as a plausible reconstruction rather than a recorded one. A commoner register name.

name: Osato
explanation: Osato - Derived from the phrase "the village of one's birth", this name embodies the idea of home as the place one carries everywhere. It is often associated with those who stay close to their kin, welcome strangers as guests, and never forget the road back.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Sato, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Sato is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 里 (sato, "village, hometown"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name.

name: Okin
explanation: Okin - Composed of the elements "honored" and "gold", this name symbolizes a daughter treasured like coin in a household that has little. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of prosperity, brightness, and lasting worth.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kin, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kin is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 金 (kin, "gold, money"), its ordinary on-reading, which is how the register name was read. A commoner register name.

name: Yone
explanation: Yone - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Eighty-eight labors in every grain", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value hard work, gratitude for the harvest, and respect for the hands that feed the Empire.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and among the most common: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana (よね) and as 米. Kanji 米 (yone, "rice"), the older kun reading of the character that survives in names. A commoner register name.

name: Saki
explanation: Saki - Stemming from the word "saku", which denotes blossoming, this name embodies the spirit of a flower opening at its proper hour. It resonates with those who are lively, hopeful, and quick to brighten a room.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, and village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima), written in kana as さき. The most conventional kanji is 咲 (saki, "to bloom"), a standard name reading; 先 (saki, "ahead, first") is a traditional alternative. A commoner register name. Saki is a very common modern given name.

name: Otsuya
explanation: Otsuya - This name is inspired by the natural element of moonlight on still water, symbolizing luster and quiet radiance. It is often chosen for its connection to polished, glowing surfaces and its representation of grace, charm, and a beauty that does not shout.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Tsuya, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Tsuya is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 艶 (tsuya, "gloss, luster, charm"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name.

name: Okiku
explanation: Okiku - A name derived from the fusion of "the chrysanthemum's late bloom" and "its long-lasting flower", reflecting a balance between patience and endurance. It is often embraced by those who strive for a dignity that ripens with age rather than fading.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kiku, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kiku is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 菊 (kiku, "chrysanthemum"), its ordinary on-reading. A commoner register name. Okiku is also the wronged servant of the ghost story Bancho Sarayashiki, who counts plates from a well, a real association most Japanese readers know.

name: Omatsu
explanation: Omatsu - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of bonsai, this name represents the pine trained for decades into a shape that looks like a mountain's own work. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patience measured in generations and have a deep respect for gardeners whose trees outlive them.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Matsu, an attested Edo commoner name and one of the most common; O-Matsu is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 松 (matsu, "pine"), a plain kun reading; the pine stands for constancy and long life. A commoner register name.

name: Beniya
explanation: The name Beniya is associated with the famous Crimson Harvest, in which the safflower fields of a northern province bloomed so richly one year that the dye paid off a decade of the domain's debts, and the daimyo remitted the villages' taxes in thanks. Those who choose this name try to embody values of industry, shared prosperity, and beauty that also feeds a household.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a dye or color name joined to the -ya ending seen in register names like Tsuya. Kanji 紅弥 (beni "safflower red, rouge" + 弥 ya "ever more, increasingly"), both ordinary readings, though the combination is stylized; be aware that 紅屋 (Beniya) is the far more usual parse, a rouge-seller's shop name. A commoner-style name.

name: Iyako
explanation: Iyako - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Increase, an event that emphasizes offering the first sheaf of the harvest so that next year's yield will grow ever greater. People choose this name to reflect their values for growth, abundance, and the steady improvement of a household's fortunes.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 彌子, read Iyako, using the old form 彌 of modern 弥; the on-reading is Bishi. 彌 means "ever more, increasingly" (kun reading iya, as in iyamasu) and 子 is the feminine suffix; the kun reading is genuine but unfamiliar to modern readers, so flag it as archaic. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Shina
explanation: Shina - This name represents grace and refinement of bearing and is often chosen by those who are raised to carry themselves with quiet dignity or who are expected to bring good manners and good standing to the family they marry into.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo lists and late-Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana as しな. Conventional kanji 品 (shina, "grace, refinement, quality"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name.
